The fragment you provided is a snippet of the FOOTiNG Foundations manual’s table of contents, specifically from chapter 6. It systematically lists sub-sections that deal with verification and design checks of foundations—both isolated and strip types—within the SOFiSTiK Structural Desktop (SSD) environment. In a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) setting, you would index each row by its section number, title, page pointer and key topic, so that queries about “soil pressure” or “sleeve design” can be routed directly to the correct passage. Below is a detailed breakdown:

1. Context  
   - Manual: FOOTiNG Foundations, Service Pack 2025-4, Build 146  
   - Issuer: SOFiSTiK AG, Nuremberg, Germany  
   - Chapter 6 covers the “Design and Verification” routines invoked by the SSD task FOOTiNG.  

2. Table Structure  
   • Column 1: Section numbers (6.2.3 through 6.6)  
   • Column 2: Section titles (“sleeve”, “Moment-V.”, etc.)  
   • Column 3: Page references (6-1 to 6-5)

3. Sections and Content Descriptions  
   6.2.3 sleeve (p. 6-1)  
   - Defines how foundations interfacing with a column sleeve are treated.  
   - Likely covers load transfer from the superstructure into the footing through a pipe or reinforcement casing.  
   - May include parameters for sleeve stiffness, embedment depth and associated limit states.  

   6.2.4 Moment-V. (p. 6-2)  
   - “Moment-V.” stands for moment verification under combined loading.  
   - Checks second-order (P-Δ) effects, biaxial bending moments (Mx, My) and resulting eccentricities.  
   - Describes the formation of design combinations and the calculation of amplified moments.  

   6.3 Permissible Soil Pressure (p. 6-3)  
   - Explains how to select or compute allowable bearing pressures according to DIN 1054:2010-12.  
   - Offers tables 1–6 from the German standard or user-defined input options.  
   - May include safety factors, geotechnical categories and soil classification guidelines.  

   6.4 Soil Pressure/Buckling (p. 6-3)  
   - Presents checks for bearing-capacity failure and overall stability (overturning, sliding).  
   - Contains algorithms for buckling under lateral loads or combined axial and moment actions.  
   - Likely discusses eccentricity limits and pressure distribution shapes (triangular, trapezoidal).  

   6.5 Design (p. 6-4)  
   - Core reinforcement design module for bending, shear and punching shear.  
   - Details calculation steps for required bar areas, spacing, concrete cover and punching shear perimeters.  
   - Covers both single (isolated) and combined footing layouts (group footings).  

   6.6 Sleeve Design (p. 6-5)  
   - Dedicated section on sizing and reinforcement of sleeves embedded in footings.  
   - Covers design checks for axial load, bending, shear and possible torsion in the sleeve region.  
   - Specifies detailing rules (development length, lap splices, corrosion allowances).

4. RAG-Friendly Indexing Suggestions  
   - Key fields: section_id, title, page, topic_tags (e.g. “soil_pressure,” “foundation_design,” “punching_shear,” “sleeve”).  
   - Short summaries or bullet points under each entry can be stored as metadata for quick retrieval.  
   - Cross-refs: link 6.3/6.4 with the geotechnical tables and 6.2.x with the structural input dialogue in SSD.

By capturing section numbers, titles, page pointers and concise topic summaries, you enable precise retrieval of design routines—whether a user asks “Where do I find punching shear checks?” or “How is allowable soil pressure determined?”—directly in your RAG vector store.

The screenshot shows the “SOFiSTiK: Fundament” dialog, divided into two main areas. On the left is a 3-D visualization of a column footing; on the right is the “System” tab, where the designer specifies material properties, positioning and general control options for all proof and calculation routines.

Left-hand 3-D View  
• A two-stage footing is shown: a central column rises from a smaller upper pad, which in turn sits on a larger base slab.  
• Load Case 2 (“Lastfall 2”) is active, as indicated by the title above the model.  
• A large blue arrow points downward at the top of the column, annotated “673” (representing a vertical load, e.g. in kN).  
• A red arrow on the side of the upper pad, labeled “286,” indicates a horizontal shear force.  
• A small blue arrow of magnitude “20” on the edge of the base slab indicates a horizontal force in the orthogonal direction.  
• Base‐plate contact pressures or soil reactions are illustrated by a grid of small dots beneath the larger footing.  
• Plain black arrows at two corners of the base slab are annotated “0.00,” showing zero bending moments at those edges or corners.  
• A black arrow at the underside of the upper pad is annotated “1.55,” likely indicating a moment or uplift reaction.  
• In the lower-left corner is the view-direction triad with red X, green Y and blue Z axes.  
• Below the 3-D window are simple view‐manipulation icons (rotate, pan, zoom) and a checkbox “Subsoil layers,” which is ticked.  
• At the very bottom of the dialog is a global checkbox “Process immediately,” also ticked, indicating each change triggers an instant recalculation.

Right-hand “System” Tab  
1. Material section  
   • Concrete: “1 C 25/30” (i.e. C25/30 per EN 206, designated concrete class)  
   • Reinforcement: “2 B 500 A” (high‐yield bar steel grade B500A)  

2. Position section  
   • “Brief description,” “Node,” and “Coordinates: X, Y, Z” – all input fields are currently empty, ready to receive a textual label or a reference node number and its coordinates in the model space.

3. General section  
   • “Consider dead load as base load” – this checkbox is enabled, meaning self-weight will be included as the base line load.  
   • Rounding foundation: a numeric field (default 0.05 m) that sets the rounding increment for automatic foundation sizing.  
   • Critical cut: a field where either “iterative” (the default) or a user‐defined factor (e.g. “1.4·d”) can be entered. With “iterative,” the software locates the worst‐case punching cone for punching shear assessment.  
   • Reinforcement: specifies the average longitudinal reinforcement ratio ρ [%] within the circular cut at 1.5·d. A default of 0.0 % means the program derives this ratio from the calculated rebar layout.  
   • Load increase factor: here the user can override the program’s automatic determination of β (which by default is at least 1.1 if no moments exist, or else is computed per German “Heft 600”).  
   • Design section: a drop-down list for selecting the location of the bending‐design cut in the foundation. Possible choices include “edge of column,” “mid of column,” “mid of column smoothed,” “mid of sleeves flank” and “edge of sleeve.”  

Tabs at the top of the panel (“System,” “Geometry,” “Proof,” “Design,” “Output,” etc.) imply subsequent steps where soil proofs (per EN 1997-1) and concrete proofs (per EN 1992-1-1) are selected, results are computed and the extent of report output is configured. The dialog neatly integrates geometry, material selection, proof settings and immediate processing, streamlining the complete foundation‐design workflow within SOFiSTiK.

In the tab System general information about the foundation are set, for example position title and the selection of materials for concrete and steel and all information for control of the proofs and calculation.
 In the section ”General” the following control options are available:
 • Rounding foundation: Rounding value for the automatic determination of foundation size (default 0.05 m)
 • Critical cut: Distance of the critical perimeter for the punching shear. With the default setting ”iterative” the program automatically calculates the worst punching cone. For special situations or comparative calculations, alternatively a factor can be entered (e.g. 1.4*d).
 • Reinforcement: Average longitudinal reinforcement level ρ in [%] within the circular cut 1.5d. With the default setting 0.0 [%] the level of the reinforcement in round cut 1.5d is determined from the calculated reinforcement.
 • Load raise factor: The load raise factor β takes into account the effect of moments in the loaded area. For special situations or comparative analyzes alternatively here can be entered a factor.
 Default: If no moments exist, the program sets β=1.1 as a minimum, otherwise the load raise factor β is determined according to the German "Heft 600".
 • Design section: Here the location for the dimensioning cut (bending design foundation)
 is specified. The following design sections are available:
 ◦ edge of column
 ◦ mid of column
 ◦ mid of column smoothed
 ◦ mid of sleeves flank
 ◦ edge of sleeve
 In section ”Proof” the desired proofs for soil according to DIN EN 1997-1 are selected. The selected proofs are executed and transferred to the result. The extend of output is controlled in the tab ”Output”.
 In the section ”Design” the required proofs for the reinforced concrete according to DIN EN 1992-1-1: 2013-04 are selected. In particular, a punching check can be enforced, even if the shear check will be decisive.

• The pedestal consists of a smaller block directly beneath the column and a slightly larger block beneath that, both rendered in darker gray tones. Beneath these is the broad, lighter‐gray base slab.

• Three orthogonal axes are indicated at the lower left corner of this view: X (red), Y (green), Z (blue). A coordinate triad icon with colored arrows marks the global orientation.  
• Three load vectors are illustrated:  
  – A large blue arrow pointing downward from the top of the column, labeled “573” (Load Case 2: Lastfall 2).

• Elevation callouts of “0.00” appear at the ground‐plane level, and “–1.55” marks the bottom of the base slab.

Right half – Geometry Tab  
• A simplified top‐down (plan) graphic shows three concentric rectangles representing the footing slab (outer), the pedestal (middle), and the column base (inner).  
• The outer rectangle is highlighted in green. Dimension arrows flank it:  
  – A vertical arrow at left indicates the Y-direction width of “200” units.  
  – A horizontal arrow at bottom indicates the X-direction width of “300” units.  
• Inside the plan graphic, the middle and inner rectangles are shown in light gray and black outlines, respectively, aligning centrally within the green outer boundary.

Caption  
At the very bottom of the image, outside the dialog window, is the label “Figure 2.2.”  

Context (from accompanying text)  
• In this “Geometry” tab, engineers specify the foundation type and set its overall plan dimensions (bx, by), plus axis distances for reinforcement design.  
• The lock‐symbols enable locking these dimensions. If a ground‐capacity verification fails and both locks are open, the software will proportionally enlarge bx and by to meet requirements.

In the tab ”Geometry” the type of foundation and its dimensions are set, as well as the axis distance for the reinforcement design.
 Predefined dimensions of the foundation can be set using the lock-symbol. In case one of the ground proof is not successfully complied and both lock-symbols are opened, the correspond- ing foundation widths are increased, holding the given proportion bx/by.

The screenshot shows the SOFiSTiK “Fundament” dialog in the process of defining and analyzing a reinforced‐concrete column foundation. Visually, the left side of the window displays a three‐dimensional model of a stepped pad foundation with an eccentric rectangular column rising from its top. The model sits above a dashed‐line plane representing the base or ground level. Just above the column, a blue arrow labeled “573” points downward, indicating a vertical compressive load of 573 kN (Load Case 2: Lastfall 2). To the right of the column, a smaller blue arrow labeled “20” indicates a 20 kN horizontal shear force in the positive x-direction. Behind the column, a red arrow marked “286” suggests a horizontal shear force of 286 kN, likely acting in the y-direction (into the screen). A black bent arrow at the lower front left of the pad shows a moment of 1.55 kN·m, indicating a small tipping moment about the base. A tri‐axis symbol with red X-axis, green Y-axis, and blue Z-axis sits at the model’s lower left corner, clarifying orientation.

Beneath the 3D view area, a “View” toolbar offers icons for rotating or translating the view (FX, FY, FZ toggles and a zoom tool), and a checkbox “Subsoil layers” is ticked, signaling that soil strata are displayed or accounted for in the calculation. A “Process immediately” box at the bottom left is also checked, meaning results will update as parameters change.

On the right side of the dialog, two tabs appear: “System” (active) and “Geometry”. The “Geometry” panel shows a plan‐view drawing of the stepped foundation with dimension callouts: the outer edge measures 110 cm in the x-direction and 60 cm in the y-direction. Concentric rectangles illustrate the intermediate footing level and the column cross‐section (highlighted in red). Dashed centerlines mark the reference axes.

Below the drawing, material and section properties are set: the “Material” field is filled with “Concrete: 3 C 45/55 (E…)”, specifying a high‐strength concrete class. Under “Cross Section,” the type is “Rectangle” with dimensions cx = 0.600 m (column width in x) and cy = 0.400 m (column width in y). This panel likely corresponds to the “Column” tab mentioned in the user’s note, where all dimensions and materials tied to the column‐foundation connection are defined automatically when possible.

Taken together, the screenshot illustrates the definition of an eccentric column—offset from the foundation center—and the means by which the software will automatically adjust foundation dimensions based on user‐entered eccentricities e and ey. Positive values shift the column in the positive x or y direction, while negative values shift it oppositely, all measured either from the foundation edge or center as governed by user settings.

All information related to a columnn connected to the coundation is located in the tab ”Column”. The dimensions and materials are taken automatically when it is possible.
 In case an eccentric column, there are two possibilities to control the automatic increase of the foundation dimensions.
 The values of e and ey will be measured from the outer foundation edge and mantained during the calculation. A positive value refers to the right side, a negative one to the left side.
 The values of e and ey will be relative to the center of the foundation. A positive value of e displace the column in positive x-direction.

The screenshot shows the “SOFiSTiK: Fundament” dialog, split into two main panels: a 3-D visualization on the left and a geometry-input area on the right. Below is a structured, detailed description of what is visible, suitable for indexing in a RAG vector store:

1. Window Title and Tabs  
   • Title bar reads “SOFiSTiK: Fundament.”  
   • Immediately below the title are three tabs: “System,” “Geometry” (currently active), and “Sleeve” (grayed-out).  
   • A contextual note (not part of the GUI) reminds the user that “All information related to the geometry of a sleeve foundation is located in the tab ‘Sleeve.’ The tab is disabled for foundations without sleeve.”

2. Left Panel – 3-D Model Viewer  
   • Load Case label above the model: “Load Case 2 : Lastfall 2.”  
   • A stepped foundation assembly rendered in shaded 3-D:  
     – Bottom element is a wide, flat footing block.  
     – Above this is a smaller, central pedestal block.  
     – A narrow, square-section column rises from the pedestal.  
   • Load arrows and values:  
     – A large blue arrow pointing downward at the top of the column with the numeric label “573.”  
     – A smaller red arrow acting horizontally on the pedestal with the label “286.”  
     – A small blue horizontal arrow labeled “20” pointing along a reference plane adjacent to the footing.  
     – A downward offset arrow at a corner of the footing with value “1.55” (likely soil settlement or load reaction).  
   • Coordinate triad in lower-left corner showing X (red), Y (green), Z (blue).  
   • Along the bottom of the panel:  
     – A row of view-control icons (orbit, pan, zoom, fit view).  
     – A checkbox labeled “Subsoil layers” (checked).  
     – A “Process immediately” checkbox (checked) at the very bottom.

3. Right Panel – Geometry Input  
   • At top, a 2-D plan view sketch:  
     – Outermost square representing the footing outline, with an overall horizontal dimension of “130.”  
     – Inside, a concentric square (in blue) indicating the cavity or hollow core of a sleeve foundation.  
     – A rectangular sleeve element (brown) centered within the inner square.  
     – Dimension lines showing a 25 mm offset from each outer edge to the inner square.  
   • Below the sketch, two input groups:  
     – “Wall thickness” with fields labeled “wx:” and “wy:,” each set to “0.20” (presumably meters).  
     – “Height” with subfields “outside:” and “inside:,” both currently blank.  
   • The “Sleeve” tab to the right of “Geometry” is disabled—consistent with the note that it only becomes active when a sleeve foundation is defined in a way that requires separate geometry entry.

Overall, the interface provides a combined visual and parametric specification of a stepped foundation with an embedded sleeve. The 3-D viewer confirms load magnitudes and directions, while the Geometry pane captures plan-view dimensions, wall thicknesses, and vertical heights. This structured snapshot will allow a RAG system to retrieve both visual and numeric foundation parameters, as well as to flag that sleeve-specific details must be entered (or retrieved) under the dedicated Sleeve tab when appropriate.
All information related to the geometry of a sleeve foundation is located in the tab ”Sleeve”. The tab is disabled for foundations without sleeve.

The screenshot is taken from the “SOFiSTiK: Fundament” dialog, specifically showing the Subsoil settings in the “System” tab. It can be broken into two major areas: a 3-D visualisation on the left, and a series of input controls on the right for defining the bore profile, soil pressures, subsoil layers and groundwater level.

Left-Hand 3-D View  
• A grey concrete foundation block sits on top of a larger base slab; a vertical rectangular shaft (column) rises from its centre.  
• Three force vectors are attached to the shaft/base assembly:  
  – A blue, downward-pointing arrow on its top face labelled “573” (presumably kN)  
  – A red, horizontal arrow on the left side of the shaft marked “286”  
  – A smaller blue, horizontal arrow on the right side marked “20”  
• Around the edges of the base slab the plan-view corner coordinates are shown as “0.00,” illustrating the local origin.  
• At one corner of the view there is a small triad showing the global X, Y, Z axes in red, green and blue.  
• Immediately below the model are five view-control buttons (for rotating about X, Y, Z, panning and zooming) and a checkbox labelled “Subsoil layers” (which is ticked).  
• At the very bottom left of the dialog is another checkbox labeled “Process immediately,” also checked.

Right-Hand Input Panel  
1. Bore Profile  
   • Labeled “Bore Profile,” with a combo-box showing “1 Bohrprofil” selected. To its right is a small button (ellipses) presumably to open the Bore Profile manager.  
2. Soil Pressure / Embedding Depth  
   • Under “Soil Pressure” there is an unchecked “Anchoring Depth” checkbox.  
   • Below it is a scrollable list of embedment depths in meters: 0.300, 0.500, 1.000, etc.  
3. Soil Layers Table  
   • A section labeled “Soil Layers” with a single row of data:  
     – z [m] = 0.000  
     – φ [°] = 30.0  
     – [kN/m²] (soil resistance) – blank or default value  
   • Above the table is a checkbox “Friction A δk” (currently unchecked).  
4. Groundwater Level  
   • A labeled input “Groundwater Level:” with an empty field or an up/down spinner.  

Context-Sensitive Features (as described in the accompanying text)  
• The user can choose a predefined soil profile from the “Bore Profile” list—these profiles come from the earlier “Bore profile” task.  
• Design values for soil resistance may be taken from the standard DIN 1054:2010-12 Tables A6.1–A6.8, or the user can supply their own table.  
• Instead of a full table, the user may specify a single permissible soil resistance (default 210 kN/m²).  
• Multiple soil layers can be entered; they are visualized in the 3-D window when the “Subsoil layers” box is ticked.  
• The location of the groundwater table may be defined for pore-water pressure effects.  
• A uniform additional load (permanent or variable) can be applied to the foundation: permanent loads are included in every soil verification, whereas variable loads trigger two separate checks, with and without that load.

Overall, this interface allows the engineer to couple the geometrical model of a shallow foundation with detailed subsoil parameters—borehole stratigraphy, soil strength tables or user-defined values, groundwater depth, and external loads—while immediately visualizing the resultant soil layers and load arrows in a 3-D preview.

In tab ”Subsoil” all values related to the soil are set.
 • In a combo box you can select a soil profile, which has been previously defined in the task ”Bore profile”.
 • The design values of soil resistance can be selected from the Tables A6.1 - A6.8 (DIN 1054:2010-12).
 • A user defined table is also allowed.
 • A permissible soil resistance can be defined instead of a table (default 210 [kN/m2]).
 • Several soil layer can be taken into account, they are represented in the corresponding graphic.
 • The location of the ground water level will be considered.
 A uniform additional load can be defined for the foundation.
 • Permanent: The load will be consider as permanent for the soil verification.
 • Variable: every soil verification will be performed once with the variable load and once
 without it.

The screenshot shows the SOFiSTiK “Fundament” (Foundation) module in its default “System” tab, combining a 3D visualization of a simple footing assembly on the left with a set of code‐based safety‐factor inputs on the right. Visually, the model consists of a square spread footing (bottom block), a central pedestal (middle block), and a column stub (top block). The elements are rendered in solid gray tones against a light blue background. A dotted ground‐surface plane is shown intersecting the top of the footing, and a triad of colored axes (X in red, Y in green, Z in blue) is drawn at the lower left corner of the view to indicate orientation.

Three reaction arrows illustrate the applied design loads:
 • A large vertical blue arrow pointing downward at the top of the column, labeled “573,” denotes a 573 kN (or equivalent unit) compressive load.  
 • A horizontal red arrow on the left side of the pedestal, labeled “280,” represents a lateral load of 280 kN.  
 • A smaller horizontal blue arrow on the right side of the ground plane, labeled “20,” marks a 20 kN lateral action.  

Additional numeric annotations “0.00” appear at two corners of the ground plane, indicating reference elevations, while “1.55” is stamped on the left face of the footing, likely denoting its thickness or a depth coordinate.

Beneath the 3D view is a compact toolbar offering standard view controls—rotate about X, Y or Z, zoom, pan—and a checkbox for “Subsoil layers,” which is ticked to display underlying strata. At the very bottom left, a “Process immediately” checkbox is also engaged, signaling that changes propagate to the analysis engine in real time.

On the right side, under the “System” tab header, the “Design Situations” section lists three code‐defined scenarios, each with an associated checkbox:
 • BS-P – persistent situation  
 • BS-T – transient situation  
 • BS-A – accidental situation  
All three checkboxes are currently disabled (grayed out), reflecting that these design situations and their safety factors are predefined by the selected Design Code and should generally remain unchanged.

Below this, two grouped input areas specify “Safety factors of actions” and “Safety factors of resistance,” each subdivided for the BS-P situation. 3. Load transfer into sleeve and footing

Below is a breakdown of every control code, its purpose, units and default:

1. SAVE  
  • Description: Save all design results into the central database (CDB).  
  • Unit: LIT (logical flag)  
  • Default: NEIN (NO)  

2. IMPO  
  • Description: Import system data (loads, geometry, etc.) from the CDB.  No recalculations occur while importing.  
  • Unit: LIT  
  • Default: NEIN  

3. DMII  
  • Description: If delta‐moments & delta‐forces are provided for characteristic loads, include them by addition; otherwise ignore.  
  • Unit: –  
  • Default: YES  

4. BEM  
  • Description: Force the creation of bending reinforcement even if purely geometric checks would not require it.  
  • Unit: –  
  • Default: NO  

5. FKDU  
  • Description: Factor to control the size of the punching cone (per EN 1992-1-1:2013).  A value of 0 instructs the program to compute the most unfavorable cone itself.  
  • Unit: –  
  • Default: 2.36  

6. KLAF  
  • Description: For a two-thirds core check, allow “gapping” of the core value (YES) or enforce no gap (NO).  
  • Unit: –  
  • Default: YES  

7. EGZ  
  • Description: Include self-weight and any additional (dead or live) loads in the analysis.  
  • Unit: –  
  • Default: YES

  • Description: Angle factor for a “round cut” detailing region around the column: 1.5 d (≈33.7°) or 1.0 d (45°).  
  • Unit: –  
  • Default: 1.5

  • Description: Coefficient governing the moment‐effect in the punching area.  According to EN 1992-1-1 the program will override and use its own factor if no moments act.  
  • Unit: –

Each of these fields is an integer index pointing back to a material or soil‐profile definition you have already declared elsewhere in your AQUA input deck.  Because they are purely references, all four fields are dimensionless (unit “–”) and have no hardwired defaults; you must supply explicit indices for each.

1. FOOT  
   • Description: Material number of the foundation (footing) concrete.  
   • Role: When you list multiple concrete materials under MATF (e.g. “CONC 1 C 45” for C45/55 concrete), you assign each a unique index.  The FOOT parameter tells AQUA which of those indices to use for the footing itself.  
   • Values: Any positive integer corresponding to a previously defined CONC entry.  
   • Unit: – (index)  
   • Default: – (mandatory input)

2. STEE  
   • Description: Material number of the reinforcing steel.  
   • Role: In your MATF section you define steel grades (e.g. “STEE 2 B 500A”).  The STEE index picks which of these steel grades becomes the reinforcement material for the footing design (post‐tensioning, shear links, main bars, etc.).  
   • Values: Any positive integer matching an earlier STEE entry.  
   • Unit: – (index)  
   • Default: – (mandatory input)

3. COLU  
   • Description: Material number of the column.  
   • Role: If your footing carries one or more columns, AQUA needs to know what concrete grade those columns use.  You supply this via COLU, pointing at the appropriate CONC index (could be the same as or different from the footing’s CONC).  
   • Values: Any integer linked to an existing CONC definition.  
   • Unit: – (index)  
   • Default: – (mandatory input)

4. PROF  
   • Description: Number of the soil profile.  
   • Role: Bearing‐failure and sliding checks require subsurface data.  In the “HEAD Soil Profile” section you declare one or more BORE blocks (e.g. “BORE 1… TITL ‘Bohrprofil01’”), each with layered soil parameters.  PROF indicates which soil‐profile index to associate with this footing.

The table in question defines a compact, fixed-schema record for describing discrete “actions” in a safety-oriented risk-assessment system (often referenced alongside tables named MATF and ACT). Each row represents one action entry characterized by seven core attributes. Below is a field-by-field breakdown:

1. Item (column header):  
   – Serves as the internal identifier for each attribute. It is not a data field but labels the seven parameters documented in the table.

2. Description:  
   – A human-readable summary of what each attribute means. For example, “Type of the action” or “Combination value quasi permanent.”  

3. Unit:  
   – Specifies the data format or literal length.  
     • TYPE uses LIT2, indicating a two-character literal (e.g., codes from “01” to “99” or short enumerations).  
     • TIT uses LIT32, a free-form string up to 32 characters.  
     • GAMF, GAMU, PSI0, PSI1, PSI2 carry no unit (marked “—”) because they are dimensionless safety factors or indices.

4. Default:  
   – Lists the default value assigned when no explicit value is provided.  
     • For TYPE, GAMF, GAMU, PSI0, PSI1, and PSI2, the default is “*,” signaling a mandatory field or requiring user override.  
     • TIT defaults to “’0,” a placeholder indicating “no description provided” or a system-recognized null.

Core Fields Explained:

• TYPE  
  – Purpose: Categorizes the action by an internal code (e.g., maintenance step, emergency response, periodic inspection).  
  – Usage: Cross-references higher-level process tables (MATF for material factors, ACT for action definitions) to ensure consistency across modules.

• GAMF (Favourable Safety Factor)  
  – Purpose: Captures any multiplier or coefficient that reduces risk under ideal circumstances.  
  – Range/Scale: Typically a decimal between 0.01 and 1.00; smaller values indicate stronger “favourable” mitigation.

• GAMU (Unfavourable Safety Factor)  
  – Purpose: Represents penalty factors when conditions exacerbate hazard (e.g., poor visibility, degraded equipment).  
  – Range/Scale: Values ≥1.00; larger numbers reflect increased risk.

• PSI0, PSI1, PSI2 (Combination Values)  
  – Purpose: Define the probability of occurrence or risk combination under three exposure regimes:  
     • PSI0 – rare exposure  
     • PSI1 – frequent exposure  
     • PSI2 – quasi-permanent exposure  
  – Range/Scale: Dimensionless indices, often between 0.00 and 3.00; values climb as exposure frequency increases.

• TIT (Description of the Action)  
  – Purpose: A concise, human-readable label or narrative for the action.  
  – Format: Up to 32 characters, free text. Examples: “Lubricate valve assembly,” “Evacuation drill,” “High-temp seal inspection.”

Interrelationships & Usage Notes  
– In a typical risk‐assessment workflow, TYPE determines which GAMF/GAMU defaults apply; these factors feed into a composite risk score computed via MATF and ACT reference tables.  
– The PSI values adjust that score according to how often personnel or equipment face the specified hazard.  
– TIT provides audit-trail clarity, ensuring that any automated score or factor applied can be traced back to a human­-legible action name.  

By maintaining strict unit definitions and defaults (especially “*” for mandatory overwrite), the schema enforces data integrity while offering enough flexibility to accommodate a wide variety of safety-critical procedures.

The table is a compact specification of the partial‐safety and load‐case parameters used when designing anchored structural elements in accordance with European and German standards (DIN EN 1990:2010-12 and DIN 1054:2010-12). All quantities are dimensionless “factors” (unit “–”) that are applied to loads, actions or resistances; the “Default” column gives the typical values to be stored in your RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) vector database. Below is a detailed, row-by-row breakdown:

1. Item: LC  
   • Description: “Design situation, loading.”  
   • Unit: – (dimensionless)  
   • Default: 1  
   • Notes: LC is the load‐case index. In the broader context of DIN 1054 you would typically see LC = 1 for the persistent (BS-P) scenario, LC = 2 for transient (BS-T) and LC = 3 for accidental (BS-A). In this particular table only LC = 1 is shown, meaning the default configuration refers to the main “persistent” design case.

2. Item: GAMG  
   • Description: “Safety factor of actions, permanent (DIN EN 1990).”  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: 1.35  
   • Notes: This gamma factor multiplies all permanent (dead) loads in the limit‐state design. It ensures a safety margin for uncertainties in weight, material properties, and construction tolerances.

3. Item: GAMQ  
   • Description: “Safety factor of actions, variable (DIN EN 1990).”  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: 1.50  
   • Notes: This is the partial factor for imposed, live or environmental loads (snow, wind, traffic, etc.). It is higher than GAMG to reflect greater variability and unpredictability.

4. Item: LAGU  
   • Description: “Position stability (DIN EN 1990) – unfavorable.”  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: 1.10  
   • Notes: The factor applied to unfavorably‐acting loads when checking stability (e.g., overturning or uplift).  

5. Item: LAGF  
   • Description: “Position stability (DIN EN 1990) – favorable.”  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: 0.90  
   • Notes: The factor for favorably‐acting loads during the same stability checks. Using a factor less than 1.0 for favorable loads balances the increased factor on unfavorable ones.

6. Item: WIGR  
   • Description: “Safety factors of resistances – bearing (base failure) (DIN 1054).”  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: 1.40  
   • Notes: The partial‐safety factor applied to the soil’s bearing capacity or foundation resistance. Conforms to German standard DIN 1054’s guidance for geotechnical resistances.

7. Item: WIGL  
   • Description: “Safety factors of resistances – sliding resistance (DIN 1054).”  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: 1.10  
   • Notes: The factor for shear or sliding resistance along potential failure planes. Again, taken from DIN 1054:2010-12.

Additional Context (anchoring depth):  
– The table sits within a broader chapter on “BESI – Safety factors.”  
– If the anchoring depth in the ground exceeds 2.00 m, soil‐specific weight must be recorded; deeper embedment may change safety assessments for sliding and bearing.  
– In a complete RAG vector store implementation, you would index each of these item codes (LC, GAMG, GAMQ, LAGU, LAGF, WIGR, WIGL) along with the standard reference (DIN EN 1990 or DIN 1054) and the design situation (persistent, transient, accidental) as metadata for rapid retrieval during automated design checks.

It is structured as follows:

Columns  
• “Action” – differentiates between the two fundamental categories of load effects:  
    – permanent (dead) actions, e.g. self-weight of structural or soil elements  
    – variable (live) actions, e.g. traffic loads, wind, snow, water pressure  
• “BS-P” – Partial safety factor for the Persistent (quasi-permanent) situation  
• “BS-T” – Partial safety factor for the Transient (frequently varying) situation  
• “BS-A” – Partial safety factor for the Accidental situation  

Rows  
• permanent:  
    – BS-P (Persistent) = 1.35  
    – BS-T (Transient) = 1.20  
    – BS-A (Accidental) = 1.10  
• variable:  
    – BS-P (Persistent) = 1.50  
    – BS-T (Transient) = 1.30  
    – BS-A (Accidental) = 1.10  

Key points and context  
1. Design Situations (DIN 1054:2010-12, Clause 2.2)  
   – BS-P (Persistent): represents those load combinations and environmental conditions that act continuously or for very long durations (e.g. over the service life of the structure).  
   – BS-T (Transient): covers loads that vary with time or occur periodically but are not permanent (e.g. live loads, wind gusts).  
   – BS-A (Accidental): addresses rare or exceptional events (e.g. earthquakes, ship impact, vehicle collision, blast).  

2. Partial Safety Factors (γF) for Actions  
   – These factors amplify the unfavourable effects of loads to ensure that the design remains on the “safe” side of the limit state.  
   – Permanent actions generally receive lower variable factors in the accidental case (both permanent and variable are 1.10 under BS-A) because their uncertainties under accidental loading are relatively smaller.  
   – Variable actions carry the highest factor in the persistent situation (1.50) reflecting the greater statistical scatter and unpredictability of live loads over time.  

3. Link with Resistance and Stability Checks  
   – Although not shown in this snippet, corresponding partial safety factors for resistances (γR) would be applied to soil or structural strength parameters in the same design situations.  
   – The combined use of γF (actions) and γR (resistances) ensures that the design safety margin against bearing failure, sliding, overturning, and other limit states is consistent with the partial factor method outlined in both DIN 1054 and EN 1990.  

4. Applicability in RAG Vector Store  
   – When indexing documents or records related to geotechnical or structural anchor designs, this table provides a concise reference for selecting the correct γF values for each load case.  
   – Metadata fields might include “Design Situation,” “Action Type,” and “Partial Safety Factor,” with lookup tables mapping BS-P/BS-T/BS-A to their numerical values.  
   – If anchoring depth exceeds 2 m, additional soil‐specific weight parameters must be recorded, as indicated elsewhere in the BESI input specification.  

In summary, this table codifies the standardized safety factors for permanent and variable actions across persistent, transient and accidental design situations, forming a core input to any limit-state‐based geotechnical or structural design workflow under the relevant German and European standards.

The table in question is a fragment of “Section 5.8 BESI – Safety factors” and deals specifically with the partial (safety) factors to be applied to geotechnical resistance parameters under three distinct design situations as defined by the German standard DIN 1054:2010-12. It is intended for use in limit-state design of anchored or founded structures where two failure modes—bearing failure and sliding—must be checked separately. The table’s values are to be multiplied by the characteristic resistance (e.g. ultimate bearing resistance, ultimate sliding resistance) to obtain the design resistance against each failure mode.

1. Context and Normative Reference  
   •  Standard: DIN 1054:2010-12 “Basis of geotechnical design – Foundations – Retaining structures – Embedded walls”  
   •  Section: 5.8 BESI, titled “Safety factors”  
   •  Related provisions include:  
      –  Clause 2.2 (Design Situations)  
      –  Rules for permanent vs. variable actions and combined action effects  
      –  Reference to DIN EN 1990:2010-12 for position stability and leakage checks  
   •  Note on anchoring depth: If the anchoring depth exceeds 2.00 m, an explicit record of the soil’s specific weight (unit weight) must be added.

2. Design Situations (Columns BS-P, BS-T, BS-A)  
   The table’s three columns correspond to the three “Limit States of Geotechnical Design (LC)” or “Design Situations”:  
   –  BS-P (Persistent situation): Permanent or quasi-permanent loading, e.g. dead loads, long-term groundwater conditions, sustained earth pressures.  
   –  BS-T (Transient situation): Transient or variable loading such as live loads, wind loads, seasonal groundwater variation.  
   –  BS-A (Accidental situation): Exceptional or accidental events, e.g. vehicular impact, extreme floods, seismic forces where applicable.

3. Resistance Modes (Row Labels)  
   The first column, labelled “Resistance,” identifies the two failure modes for which partial factors on resistance are specified:  
   •  Bearing Failure: The ultimate load-bearing capacity of foundations (shallow or deep) against compressive crushing or general shear.  
   •  Sliding: The resistance against horizontal shear or sliding along a base or interface, including any passive earth pressure or frictional component.

4. Partial Factors (Numerical Values)  
   Under each design situation, the partial factor γ_R for resistance is given:  
   –  For Bearing Failure  
      •  BS-P: 1.40  
      •  BS-T: 1.30  
      •  BS-A: 1.20  
   –  For Sliding  
      •  BS-P: 1.10  
      •  BS-T: 1.10  
      •  BS-A: 1.10  

5. Interpretation and Usage  
   •  To perform a geotechnical design check, characteristic resistance (R_k) is divided by the partial factor γ_R to obtain design resistance R_d = R_k / γ_R.  
   •  Higher partial factors in BS-P reflect the need for greater safety against bearing failure under long-term loads. The accidental situation allows slightly lower factors for bearing because of its short-term nature, but design must still meet stringent safety requirements.  
   •  Sliding resistance uses a uniform factor (1.10) across all situations, acknowledging that sliding is less dependent on load duration but still requires a safety margin.

6. Integration into a RAG-style Vector Store  
   When capturing this table in a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system, entries should include:  
   –  Key: “DIN 1054:2010-12 Section 5.8 – Resistance partial factors”  
   –  Metadata: Design situation codes (BS-P, BS-T, BS-A), resistance mode (bearing, sliding), normative reference  
   –  Values: Numeric safety factors for each cell  
   –  Context notes: Definitions of design situations, note on anchoring depth requirement  

By indexing each cell along with its associated design situation and failure mode, downstream queries (e.g. “What factor applies to bearing resistance under transient loading?”) can be answered directly and unambiguously.

The table defines the primary input parameters for a single‐column foundation design module. Each row corresponds to a keyword (Item), its meaning (Description), the expected unit of entry (Unit), and any preset default (Default).  Below is a breakdown of each parameter, together with relevant behavioral rules drawn from the accompanying context.

1. TYPE (Unit: LIT, Default: EINZ)  
   • Purpose: Specifies the foundation form.  
   • Allowed values:  
     – EINZ: Normal block foundation  
     – KOE: Sleeve (socket) foundation  
     – BLOC: Sleeve block‐out foundation  
     – STRE: Strip foundation (continuous footing)  
     – STIF: L-shaped (boot) foundation  
   • Impact: Drives which geometric and reinforcement checks the program applies.

2. BX (Unit: cm, Default: “!” – user‐supplied)  
   • Purpose: Foundation length in the global X direction.  
   • Behavior:  
     – BX > 0 & BY > 0: Both dims accepted as entered. No iterative resizing for soil pressure; design moves directly to punching and stability checks. If stability fails, BX/BY increase automatically.  
     – BX > 0 & BY < 0: BX fixed; BY is iterated until permissible soil pressure is not exceeded by the applied loads.  
     – BX < 0 & BY > 0: BY fixed; BX is iterated similarly.  
     – BX < 0 & BY < 0: Both BX and BY are iterated simultaneously, preserving the initial aspect ratio (|BX| : |BY|).  
     – BX = 0 & BY = 0: Both dimensions derived from the column cross‐section ratio CX : CY.

3. BY (Unit: cm, Default: “!” – user‐supplied)  
   • Purpose and rules: Analogous to BX but in the Y direction.  Sign conventions and modification logic mirror those of BX.

4. HI (Unit: cm, Default: “!” – user‐supplied)  
   • Purpose: Foundation thickness measured at the support interface (column or sleeve wall).  
   • Notes: Defined at the edge of the column or socket.  Serves as the starting depth for punching shear and flexural design.

5. HA (Unit: cm, Default: “!” – user‐supplied)  
   • Purpose: Foundation thickness at its outer edge, away from the support.  
   • Constraint: HA ≤ HI.  Tapering or stepped designs must respect this upper bound.

6. D1X (Unit: cm, Default: “!” – user‐supplied)  
   • Purpose: Concrete cover (distance from face of foundation to first layer of reinforcement) in the X direction.  Governs development length and durability.

7. D1Y (Unit: cm, Default: “!” – user‐supplied)  
   • Purpose: Analogous cover dimension in the Y direction.

8. NBEM (Unit: LIT, Default: STR)  
   • Purpose: Selects the location of the critical design section for punching shear and moment distribution.  
   • Options:  
     – STR: Section at column edge (standard)  
     – STM: Section at column centre (no rounding)  
     – AUSR: Section at column centre with corner rounding  
     – KOEM: Section at mid‐thickness of a sleeve wall  
     – KOER: Section at the outer edge of a sleeve wall  

By capturing both geometric parameters and control flags, this table directs the program to construct, adjust, and verify the foundation shape, soil‐pressure compliance, punching shear checks, and reinforcement detailing. The sign‐based rules for BX/BY allow automated resizing to meet geotechnical limits while preserving a user-specified footprint aspect ratio or linking dimensioning to the column’s own proportions (CX : CY) when both inputs are zero. In combination, HI, HA, D1X/D1Y, and NBEM complete the section‐control and cover specification necessary for a robust structural design.

Figure 5.1 is a three‐view line drawing of a sleeve (Köcher) foundation (KOE) showing its block-out, slab and plan geometry, together with the key dimensions and section cuts used for punching‐shear and structural design.

1. Cross‐section Z–Z (top view fragment)  
   – Two vertical lines at the very top represent the inside faces of the concrete sleeve or column collar.  
   – Below these lines a frustum-shaped “block-out” (BLOC) is shown: its sides slope outward as they rise, forming a truncated pyramid whose upper face is flush with the underside of the sleeve. This block-out provides space for reinforcement and grout.  
   – Immediately beneath the block-out there is the main foundation slab, drawn as a thick horizontal bar.  
   – An upward–downward arrow labelled “HX” marks the static height (HX) between the lower face of the block-out and the top surface of the slab. In design, HX (and similarly HY in the orthogonal direction) is the depth at which punching‐shear checks are performed.  
   – A pair of arrows at the bottom of this slab point downward and bear the section‐cut label “Z,” indicating that the plan view below is taken at the level Z–Z (usually at the critical shear perimeter).

2. Plan view (middle of figure)  
   – The large outer rectangle is the horizontal outline of the foundation.  
   – Inside it, a smaller, concentric square shows the plan of the concrete sleeve or column.  
   – From the centre of the sleeve, a downward arrow marked “Y” denotes the direction of the Y–Y cross–section (and also the axis along which the transverse shear or moment Y is evaluated).  
   – No internal reinforcement is sketched here, but this plane is where the critical punching shear perimeter is typically traced, at a distance Z from the column faces.

3. Cross‐section Y–Y (immediately above plan view)  
   – Two parallel lines rising from the slab represent the sleeve walls in the Y direction. They are drawn vertical, since the block-out taper appears only in the Z section.  
   – The slab’s constant overall thickness is shown by the distance between its top and bottom horizontal edges. This section confirms that outside the block-out the slab thickness is uniform along Y–Y.

4. Overall plan dimensioning (bottom of figure)  
   – A long horizontal dimension line spans the full width of the foundation and is labelled “BX.” This is the total foundation dimension in the X‐direction (always > 0), used to compute soil pressures and check bearing capacity.  
   – Two inward‐pointing arrows from each foundation edge (only one side is labelled) indicate the column or sleeve width “CX.” In practice both half‐spans from each face equal CX/2, so that CX is centred or placed eccentrically according to the SP/RAND options.  

All key variables in this multi-view plot correspond to the textual definitions in the software manual:  
- BX, BY: foundation plan sides (both positive for fixed dimensions, negative to trigger automatic sizing).  
- CX, CY: column or sleeve cross‐section dimensions (input in cm for punching checks and aspect‐ratio control).  
- HX, HY: static heights for shear design (must be less than overall slab thickness).  
- Z: section plane depth below the top of slab where critical shear perimeters are established.  
- The labels Z–Z and Y–Y specify the locations of the horizontal and transverse sections, respectively.

The illustration is a schematic, cross-sectional side view of a single-column foundation (often referred to in the source text as a “block-out” or BLOC foundation) showing the geometric relationships and key design dimensions used in the automated foundation-design program. Below is a detailed, itemized description of each graphic element and its corresponding notation:

1. Column Section  
   - A vertical rectangular stem represents the column or sleeve wall (“Kolonner”).  
   - Two horizontal arrows on either side of the stem indicate the column’s plan dimensions CX (left arrow) and CY (right arrow). These are the clear widths in the two orthogonal horizontal directions, input in centimeters.

2. Transition (Podium)  
   - At the base of the vertical stem, the sides flare outward in straight, sloping lines. This represents the transition from the column width to the broader footing base.  
   - No dimension arrows are shown on the sloping faces, but this flare corresponds to the foundation’s “strip” or “L-shaped” geometry if applicable (STRE or STIF in the source code).

3. Footing Base  
   - Beneath the sloped transition is a horizontal rectangular block: the main body of the foundation.  
   - Along its underside runs a thin line, indicating the soil interface.

4. Horizontal Dimensions  
   - BY: A horizontal double-headed arrow, centered beneath the footing, measures the total foundation width in the Y-direction (BY).  
   - EY: On the same baseline as BY, two short arrows spaced inward from the ends of BY indicate the “eccentricity” EY, i.e. the offset of the column axis from the center of the footing in the Y-direction.  
   - Z: A single-headed arrow pointing downward from the center of the footing base indicates the vertical downward force vector Z (resultant load at the column).

5. Vertical Dimensions  
   - HI: To the left of the footing, a tall double-headed arrow spans from the underside of the footing base up to the top of the transition. This is the total internal foundation thickness (HI).  
   - HA: Nested inside the HI bracket is a shorter double-headed arrow marking the external foundation thickness (HA). By code, HA must be less than or equal to HI.  
   - Both arrows are aligned with the left edge of the footing and labelled accordingly.

6. Reference Notations (in the lower right corner)  
   - “Figure 5.2” identifies the drawing number in the program documentation.

Contextual References from the Source Text  
  • BX and BY are the user-input foundation dimensions in the two horizontal directions. In the image only BY is explicitly shown—an analogous dimension BX would appear if the section were rotated 90°.  
  • If BX or BY are negative or zero in the input, the program will recompute those sides to satisfy soil-pressure and punching criteria, as described under the “no modification,” “BY is modified,” “BX is modified,” and “both modified” cases.  
  • HI is the internal slab thickness at the column or sleeve edge; HA is the external slab thickness. The design also requires static heights HX and HY (not shown in this view) for internal punching shear checks.  
  • The offset dimension EY illustrates the ability to place the column eccentrically on the foundation, using the SP (center-of-gravity) or RAND (edge-referenced) options.  
  • The sleeve parameters (SLEE) and column reinforcement parameters (COLU) would be defined elsewhere; here, the visual focuses on the outline and key dimensional controls for automated sizing.

Overall, this figure serves as the central reference for how the program reads, interprets, and adjusts the critical geometry—foundational widths BX/BY, slab thicknesses HI/HA, and eccentricities EX/EY—when automatically performing bearing-pressure, stability, punching, and reinforcement checks.

The table shown governs all user‐supplied input parameters for the “SLEE” (sleeve) element in the foundation design module. Every row corresponds to one input variable; each variable has an internal code (“Item”), a human‐readable description, the unit in which it must be entered, and a default or requirement flag. All dimensional inputs are specified in centimeters (cm). A “!” in the Default column signifies that the user must supply a value (no built‐in default), whereas any other entry is the default to be used if the field is left blank.

1. HSWO (Sleeve height outside)  
   – Description: Total vertical extent of the sleeve measured from the foundation surface to its outer top edge.  
   – Unit: cm  
   – Default: ― (user must specify)  

2. HSWI (Sleeve height inside)  
   – Description: Vertical extent of the sleeve measured from the foundation surface to its inner top edge (i.e. undercut depth).  
   – Unit: cm  
   – Default: ― (user must specify)  

3. WXWU (Upper wall thickness in X‐direction)  
   – Description: Thickness of the sleeve wall on the X‐axis side.  
   – Unit: cm  
   – Default: ― (user must specify)  

4. WYWU (Upper wall thickness in Y‐direction)  
   – Description: Thickness of the sleeve wall on the Y‐axis side.  
   – Unit: cm  
   – Default: WXWU (if not supplied, the X‐direction thickness is reused)  

5. WXGU (Gap width at the top)  
   – Description: Horizontal clearance or grout gap between column and sleeve at the sleeve’s upper edge.  
   – Unit: cm  
   – Default: ― (user must specify)  

6. WXWL (Gap width at the bottom)  
   – Description: Horizontal clearance or grout gap between column and sleeve at the sleeve’s lower edge.  
   – Unit: cm  
   – Default: ― (user must specify)  

7. TYPE (Sleeve type)  
   – Description: Surface finish of the sleeve interior and exterior. Two literal options:  
     • R = rough (default): standard concrete surface  
     • G = smooth: steel‐lined or finished interior  
   – Unit: LIT (literal)  
   – Default: R  

8. KOEB (Control sleeve design method)  
   – Description: Selects the analytical model used to check stresses and deformations in the sleeve:  
     • LEON = Leonhardt’s method (default)  
     • PSCH = Paschen (DAfStb Heft 411)  
     • STWM = beam‐structure model  
   – Unit: LIT (literal)  
   – Default: LEON  

Usage notes and interdependencies:  
- Both HSWO and HSWI must be provided; HSWI must always be less than or equal to HSWO.  
- If WYWU is omitted, the program assumes the Y‐direction thickness equals WXWU.  
- Gap widths WXGU/WXWL control the grout or packing thickness and affect load transfer; they must be chosen so that the column can be correctly centralized and grouted.  
- The TYPE setting influences friction and anchorage in bearing checks.  
- KOEB determines which code‐based or analytical procedure governs the sleeve design, influencing soil‐sleeve interaction and punching checks.

The diagram is a transverse (x–z) section through a concrete foundation with an embedded sleeve and column. It combines a sloped foundation slab on the left with a rectangular “block-out” on the right that houses the sleeve and, ultimately, the column. Key features, coordinate axes and dimensional labels are as follows:

1. Geometry and Coordinate System  
   • A red horizontal arrow (“x”) points to the left, and a red vertical arrow (“z”) points downward, defining the local coordinate axes.  
   • The overall foundation footprint is shown at the bottom by the long horizontal line, dimensioned “BX,” which spans the full width of the footing.  

2. Sloped Foundation Slab (Left)  
   • Starting at the left edge of the footing, the top surface inclines gently upward and to the right.  
   • The vertical thickness at the left end is labeled “HI” (inside foundation thickness). A vertical dimension line marks the distance from the footing bottom to the inclined top.  

3. Transition to Block-Out (Center)  
   • At a certain distance from the left, the inclined top meets a small vertical riser, which then steps inward to form the shelf for the sleeve block-out.  
   • The horizontal run from this riser to the underside of the sloped slab is marked “EZ.” This represents the overhang or cantilever in the x-direction measured from the block-out centerline back to the sloping slab.  

4. Sleeve Block-Out and Column Interface (Right)  
   • The right portion is a rectangular block-out rising from the footing base. Its internal cavity is dimensioned by “HSWI” (height inside the sleeve block) measured upward from the footing bottom to the underside of the column seat.  
   • The horizontal width of this block-out at its base is “EX,” measured from the rightmost point of the cantilevered portion to the outer edge of the sleeve block.  
   • Around the column, a sleeve wall of thickness “WX” is depicted: two close parallel lines on the right flank of the block-out. This thickness ensures a gap between column and concrete sleeve.  
   • At the very top of the block-out, a small rectangle represents the base of the column seated in the sleeve. Its centroid is offset from the right face by “CLX.”  

5. Annotation “SPT”  
   • A short leader line from the interior of the block-out marks “SPT,” indicating a reference point (e.g. the centre of gravity or design section) on the sleeve wall.  

6. Overall Notes  
   • All dimension arrows terminate in perpendicular “tick” marks. The horizontal dimensions (BX, EX, EZ, CLX) run parallel to the x-axis; vertical dimensions (HI, HSWI) run parallel to the z-axis.  
   • The drawing is captioned “Figure 5.3” at the lower right. It likely illustrates how column, sleeve, and foundation interact and where design checks (e.g., punching, soil pressure) are performed according to parameters such as HI (inside thickness), HA (outside thickness), HX/HY (static heights), and various design positions (STR, STM, KOEM, KOER).  

In summary, the figure provides a detailed cross-section of a stepped foundation that supports a sleeved column. It clearly identifies the slab thickness, overhang length, sleeve dimensions and wall thickness, and column-offset positions—all referenced to a local x–z coordinate system.

The table shown is part of the “COLU – Column” input block in a foundation‐design program. It lists the key column parameters you must specify, their meaning, units and the defaults used if you leave them blank. Below is a structured walkthrough of each field and how it ties into the rest of the foundation model.

1. General structure  
   • Item – the short code you type in to select or override this parameter.  
   • Description – what the parameter controls or represents.  
   • Unit – the physical unit expected.  
   • Default – the value or flag the program uses if you do not enter anything.

2. QA: Type of column (Unit = LIT, Default = Q4)  
   • QU: Rectangle cross section with circumferential (perimeter) reinforcement.  
   • QK: Circle cross section with circumferential reinforcement.  
   • Q4: Rectangle with rod‐bundle (corner bars) reinforcement.  
   • QS: Rectangle with bar‐bundle along one face.  
   • QR: Symmetric (uniform) reinforcement.  
   Choosing the column type affects the punching (“Loch”) and bending checks and links to the sleeve model (if you have a block‐out or sleeve foundation).

3. CX, CY: Column dimensions in the X and Y directions (cm; Defaults = 30 cm each)  
   • These define the plan‐view size of the column.  
   • They feed into two critical places:  
     – Punching shear checks at the foundation–column interface;  
     – Determining the foundation aspect ratio BX : BY when the user has not fixed BX and/or BY (see foundation‐dimension logic under “GEOM”).  
   • If both BX and BY are zero, the program will adopt CX : CY to size the footing.

4. D1: Distance of reinforcement (cm; Default = 5 cm)  
   • Covers the clear cover to the column’s longitudinal bars, measured from the column surface to the centroid of side‐bars.  
   • Influences the effective depth used in moment capacity and punching checks.

5. DU: Diameter of column reinforcement (mm; Default = 12 mm)  
   • The nominal bar size for the longitudinal reinforcement.  
   • Combined with D1, defines the effective depth to steel.

6. AS: Necessary reinforcement of column (cm²; Default = 0)  
   • Computed from factored axial loads and bending moments.  
   • Ensures the column has adequate flexural and axial capacity.

7. ASV: Available reinforcement of column (cm²; Default = 0)  
   • The amount of steel actually provided (or assumed provided) in design.  
   • Used to calculate lap‐splice lengths for the sleeve (block‐out) reinforcement and to verify that provided steel meets the required AS.

8. EX, EY, EZ: Eccentricities in X, Y, and Z directions (cm; Defaults = 0 cm)  
   • Allow you to offset the column’s centroid relative to the foundation geometry.  
   • EX/EY shift the column horizontally; EZ shifts it vertically.  
   • Nonzero values affect the lever arms in moment design of footing and punching checks.

9. EOPT: Eccentricity reference (LIT; Default = SP)  
   • RAND – eccentricity measured from the foundation edge.  
   • SP – eccentricity measured from the column’s centre of gravity.  
   • Select “RAND” if you need a fixed stand-off from the foundation perimeter, e.g., for hall columns loaded from one side.

How this ties into the broader foundation logic  
• The column inputs (CX, CY, reinforcement, eccentricity) feed directly into the footing‐dimension and design routines described under “GEOM” and “STRE.”  
• If you leave BX or BY negative or zero, the program iterates on foundation size using CX : CY ratios and soil‐pressure checks.  
• The punching verification uses D1, DU, and AS/ASV combined with footing thickness (HI, HA) and design‐section positions (NBEM options: STR, STM, AUSR, KOEM, KOER).  
• Should the stability or bearing‐pressure checks fail, BX/BY will be increased automatically and a warning printed.

In short, this table configures the column’s geometry, reinforcement and positioning, all of which drive the footing sizing, punching‐shear checks and sleeve/block‐out reinforcement detailing.

The drawing is a simplified plan‐view schematic of a rectangular foundation with its supported column and the associated eccentricities and applied forces. It is captioned “Figure 5.4” and conveys how the column centroid is offset within the footing in both principal directions and how those offsets (EX, EY) relate to the footing edges.

Overall layout  
- A large outer rectangle represents the footing (foundation) plan-view footprint.  
- A smaller inner square represents the column or sleeve wall cross-section. That square is not concentric but shifted toward the upper-left corner of the footing.  
- Two orthogonal centerlines (one vertical, one horizontal) intersect at the centroid of the column square. These crosshairs serve as the reference axes for eccentricity and for applying load vectors.

Eccentricities EX and EY  
- Along the horizontal centerline, double-headed arrows extend from the column centroid line to the left and right edges of the footing. Both arrows point inward toward the centerline and are labeled “EX.” These indicate the horizontal eccentricity: the offset distance in the X-direction between the column’s line of action and the footing centerline (or edges).  
- Along the vertical centerline, similar double-headed arrows extend upward and downward from the column centroid to the top and bottom edges of the foundation. Those are labeled “EY” and denote the vertical eccentricity in the Y-direction.

Applied loads  
- On the top edge of the footing, a single vertical arrow points downward. It is centered horizontally but offset relative to the column’s centroid, suggesting a vertical load V acting with some eccentricity in Y.  
- Inside the right side of the large rectangle, another downward arrow is drawn and labeled “VY.” This likely represents the shear force component in the Y-direction applied at the column base (or at the interface between column and footing).  
- Although not explicitly shown, by symmetry one could imagine an analogous “VX” on the lower edge if lateral shear in X were being illustrated.

Key geometric relationships implied by the sketch  
1. The column centroid does not coincide with the geometric center of the foundation.  
2. The distances EX and EY illustrate how the footing design must account for both moment‐inducing eccentricities under the applied vertical load and the lateral shear forces.  
3. By showing the offsets graphically, the figure supports the procedure described in the surrounding text for calculating footing dimensions (BX, BY) and adjusting them when BX or BY is negative (i.e. when the user wants the program to solve for necessary width or length such that bearing pressures remain within allowable limits).

How this ties into the surrounding context  
- The text defines how foundation plan dimensions BX and BY are modified depending on user input signs (positive to leave unchanged, negative to compute a dimension, both zero to derive proportions from column aspect ratio). In this sketch, EX and EY are the actual offsets that feed into calculation of moments Mx = V·EY and My = V·EX.  
- The arrows and labels correlate with the user-input variables “EX” and “EY,” which in practice one would enter under the COLU (column) or FEET (foundation) dialogue to position the column eccentrically on the footing.  
- In design routines such as punching shear checks, strip foundation analysis, or sleeve wall design, these eccentricities become critical for locating the design sections (options STR, STM, KOEM, KOER, etc.) at the proper distances from the loaded column faces.

In sum, Figure 5.4 provides a clear plan‐view representation of a rectangular footing, its offset column, the eccentricities EX and EY, and the applied vertical/shear loads, all of which form the basis for automatic adjustment of foundation dimensions and internal checks against soil pressure and structural capacity.

The table defines the schema and semantics of a “loadcase” record used in structural‐analysis or support‐reaction extraction. Each row (Item) corresponds to one field in the record; the four columns are:  
• Item – short field name  
• Description – what it represents  
• Unit – measurement unit or data type  
• Default – default value or marker if mandatory/optional  

Below is a detailed walk-through of each field, grouped by function:

1. Identification  
  • NO  
    – Number of the loadcase (integer index).  
    – Unit: none.  
    – Default: “–” (no implicit default; must be specified).  
  • TYPE  
    – Type of action (loading class). Valid literals are:  
        G = permanent loading  
        S = snow  
        Q = variable loading (A, B variants)  
        Q_A = variable loading (C, D variants)  
        Q_B = variable loading (E)  
        W = wind  
        A = außergewöhnlich (exceptional)  
    – Unit: LIT (literal text).  
    – Default: G (permanent).  
  • TIT  
    – Title or short description of the loadcase.  
    – Unit: LIT32 (up to 32‐character text).  
    – Default: “–” (optional free text).

2. Reference to Support Database  
  • KN  
    – Node number at which support reactions are read from the central database (CDB).  
    – Unit: none (integer).  
    – Default: “–” (if omitted, no database takeover).

3. First‐Order Actions (Static Loads)  
  • V  
    – Axial force along the member’s local axis. Positive = loading (tension/compression direction defined by model convention); negative = unloading.  
    – Unit: kN.  
    – Default: “!” (mandatory).  
  • MX  
    – Bending moment about the local X‐axis (moment in the Y–Z plane).  
    – Unit: kNm.  
    – Default: “–” (optional).  
  • MY  
    – Bending moment about the local Y‐axis (moment in the X–Z plane).  
    – Unit: kNm.  
    – Default: “–” (optional).  
  • HX  
    – Lateral shear force in the local X‐direction. Positive HX and negative MY share the same action sense.  
    – Unit: kN.  
    – Default: “–” (optional).  
  • HY  
    – Lateral shear force in the local Y‐direction. Positive HY and positive MX share the same action sense.  
    – Unit: kN.  
    – Default: “–” (optional).

4. Second‐Order (P-Δ / P-M) Effects  
  • DMX  
    – Equivalent second‐order bending moment about X (accounts for geometry changes under load).

The table in question defines the schema for a single load‐case entry in a structural analysis input file.  Each row in the table corresponds to one of the key fields that must be provided (or may be left at its default) when defining a “LOAD” record.  Below is a field‐by‐field rundown of what each item means, how it is used in the calculation, the units expected, and any default values or special notes.

1. NO (Number of the load)  
   • Description: A sequential identifier for this particular load case.  It allows the software to distinguish among multiple loads.  
   • Unit: none (integer index)  
   • Default: none (must be specified by the user)

2. TYPE (Type for the check)  
   • Description: Specifies which design check or limit state this load case addresses.  Valid codes are:  
     – K1 (“mid 1/3” bending check at one‐third span)  
     – K2 (“mid 2/3” bending check at two‐thirds span)  
     – GL (Sliding resistance)  
     – GB (Bearing‐failure / punching shear)  
     – LAGS (Global stability / overturning)  
     – BEME (Reinforcement design in bending)  
   • Unit: LIT (literal code field)  
   • Default: BEME

3. KN (Node number)  
   • Description: The node in the finite‐element mesh or supporting structure where the load or reaction is applied.  This must match a node defined in the CDB (central database of support points and geometry).  
   • Unit: none (integer)  
   • Default: none (mandatory input)

4. V (Axial force)  
   • Description: Axial load acting along the member’s longitudinal axis at the specified node.  A positive V is loading (compression or tension depending on element sign convention); a negative V is unloading.  
   • Unit: kN  
   • Default: “!” (exclamation mark) – indicates that this value must be supplied.

5. MY (Moment about Y axis)  
   • Description: Bending moment about the global Y axis, which produces rotation around the Y axis and corresponds to bending in the X–Z plane.  
   • Unit: kNm  
   • Default: none (zero assumed if omitted)

6. MX (Moment about X axis)  
   • Description: Bending moment about the global X axis, causing rotation around the X axis (bending in the Y–Z plane).  
   • Unit: kNm  
   • Default: none (zero assumed if omitted)

7. HX (Lateral force in X direction)  
   • Description: Transverse shear force acting in the global X‐direction.  Shares its positive sense with negative MY (both push in the same sense on the cross section).  
   • Unit: kN  
   • Default: none (zero if omitted)

8. HY (Lateral force in Y direction)  
   • Description: Transverse shear force acting in the global Y‐direction.  Its positive sense coincides with positive MX (same cross‐sectional action).  
   • Unit: kN  
   • Default: none (zero if omitted)

9. ZUGV (Additional load in Z direction)  
   • Description: Any extra vertical or out‐of‐plane force (for example, wind uplift or surcharge) acting in the Z direction at the node.  
   • Unit: kN  
   • Default: none (zero if omitted)

10. TIT (Title of the loadcase)  
    • Description: A free‐text label (up to 64 characters) that helps the engineer identify or comment on the load case in reports or on printouts.  
    • Unit: LIT64 (64‐character literal string)  
    • Default: none

The table shown is the definition of the “foundation” input record used to specify the geometric and positional parameters of a column foundation for structural‐analysis or CAD/FEA import routines (often in the context of a larger database such as LCDB or an application identified by KN).  Each row of the table corresponds to one input field, and the four columns of the table describe:

  • Item — the mnemonic or keyword used in the input file  
  • Description — a human-readable label or explanation of that keyword  
  • Unit — the expected units or data type  
  • Default — the value assumed if the field is omitted  

Because the foundation is typically a rectangular plate or block, its two principal dimensions (BX, BY) lie along local X and Y axes; a rotation (WI) can be applied if the foundation axes do not coincide with global axes.  The computational fixed-point of the column—i.e. the point through which column loads are applied—can be offset from the geometric center of the foundation by REP.  This table organizes all of those inputs in one place.

Detailed breakdown of each field:

1. NO  
   – Description: Node number  
   – Unit: none (integer identifier)  
   – Default: “*” (mandatory)  
   – Notes: References the unique node ID in the global finite‐element model to which this foundation belongs.

2. POS  
   – Description: Position description  
   – Unit: LIT8 (8-character literal string)  
   – Default: “*” (mandatory)  
   – Notes: Free-form text to classify or name the foundation (e.g. “Corner,” “Interior,” “Edge”).

3. GEO  
   – Description: Description for the same size of foundation  
   – Unit: LIT16 (16-character literal string)  
   – Default: “*” (mandatory)  
   – Notes: Can be used to tag or group foundations sharing identical dimensions and other parameters.

4. BX  
   – Description: Foundation dimension in X direction  
   – Unit: cm  
   – Default: “*” (mandatory)  
   – Notes: Defines the total width of the foundation along its local X axis.

5. BY  
   – Description: Foundation dimension in Y direction  
   – Unit: cm  
   – Default: “*” (mandatory)  
   – Notes: Defines the total length of the foundation along its local Y axis.

6. WI  
   – Description: Rotation of the foundation axis opposite to the global coordinate system  
   – Unit: degree  
   – Default: 0  
   – Notes: Positive angles rotate the local foundation axes counter-clockwise with respect to the global X–Y plane.  Use this when BX/BY are not aligned to the global grid.

7. REP  
   – Description: Computational fixed point of the column in the foundation  
   – Unit: m  
   – Default: 0  
   – Notes: A 2D or 3D vector (depending on implementation) specifying the offset from the geometric center where the column’s load is applied.  Allows eccentric loading definition.

8. TIT  
   – Description: Positionsbezeichnung (position designation in German)  
   – Unit: LIT32 (32-character literal string)  
   – Default: “*” (mandatory)  
   – Notes: Extended title or label for reporting and documentation purposes.

– KN may refer to a project or code identifier under which these foundation definitions are collected.

The input table defines the core attributes of a Structural Point in Footing (SPT), i.e. the anchor­point that ties a foundation element to its parent structural element.  All parameters are given in a local coordinate system whose origin is at the center of the upper face of the foundation (z-axis pointing downward).  This description is intended for use in a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) vector store, so that each field can be semantically indexed.

Table structure:
• Four columns:  
  – Item: the abbreviated field name  
  – Description: what the field represents  
  – Unit: physical unit or literal type  
  – Default: default value, if the field is omitted  

Detailed row‐by‐row breakdown:

1. NO  
   • Description: “Point number” – a unique integer index identifying this structural point within the footing definition.  
   • Unit: none (marked “–”).  
   • Default: “–” (no default; usually must be supplied).

2. X, Y, Z  
   • Description: “Point coordinates” in the local footing coordinate system.  
     – X: horizontal coordinate along local X-axis, positive to one side of the foundation.  
     – Y: horizontal coordinate along local Y-axis, orthogonal to X.  
     – Z: vertical coordinate measured downward from the upper face (so Z = 0.0 lies in the plane of the top of the foundation, positive downward).  
   • Unit: “[m]_1001” – meters according to unit code 1001.  
   • Default: “0.0” (if omitted, the point defaults to the origin of its local system).

3. NX, NY, NZ  
   • Description: components of the local coordinate system’s z-axis, expressed in the global coordinate system of the structural element.  This axis always points “downward” in gravity direction toward the lower face of the foundation.  
     – NX, NY, NZ are the direction cosines (unit-vector components).  
   • Unit: none (“–”) because these are dimensionless direction ratios.  
   • Default: “*” – a placeholder indicating that the user or calling application must explicitly supply a valid unit-vector.

4. SX, SY, SZ  
   • Description: components of the local coordinate system’s x-axis, again given in the global system of the connected structural element.  The local x-axis defines one in-plane horizontal direction on the top face of the foundation.  
   • Unit: none (“–”).  
   • Default: “*” – mandatory input.

5. GUID  
   • Description: “128 bit code given as hexadecimal string” – a globally unique identifier for traceability and cross-referencing.  
   • Unit: “Lit” – literal string type.  
   • Default: “!” – indicates that a GUID must always be provided; no automatic default is generated.

Contextual notes:
• All coordinates and direction‐cosines refer to a local coordinate system centered at the middle of the foundation’s top surface, independent of the structural point’s parent coordinate system.  
• The z-axis (NX,NY,NZ) and x-axis (SX,SY,SZ) together fully define orientation; the y-axis is implied by the right‐hand rule.  
• The GUID ensures each SPT entry can be unambiguously identified in a broader database or model exchange.

Usage:
When populating the vector store, each field becomes a searchable metadata attribute:
• “NO” → integer ID  
• “X/Y/Z” → 3-component position vector  
• “NX/NY/NZ” → 3-component orientation vector (down direction)  
• “SX/SY/SZ” → 3-component orientation vector (local x direction)  
• “GUID” → string identifier  
This enables downstream tasks like:
• Nearest-neighbor queries on position (X,Y,Z).  
• Orientation matching or filtering by axis direction.  
• Cross-referencing by GUID to link footings with structural elements.
